body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The subject of the new drama at this theatre, called the Royal Oak, is immediately perceived by the title of the piece. It is founded on the sufferings of Charles the Second after his defeat at Worcester, including the battle at that place, his successful shelter in an oak-tree, and his final escape back again to France. These incidents are of a nature to excite great interest; and as the author has not scrupled to represent his hero as a pattern of courage, candour, and warmth of heart, he has succeeded in awakening the attention and sympathy of the spectators to no inconsiderable degree. He is, of course, very far from confining himself to matter of fact: indeed the adventures which are recognized by the spectator as founded on the real history are coloured so as to retain little of their former complexion, and to these are super-added the most romantic fables, of which the family of Colonel Windham are made the instruments. In the house of this gentleman, Charles is represented as escaping from the search of his enemies by the heroic devotion of the Colonel's son, who, at the suggestion of his mother, disguises and delivers himself up to them. The mother afterwards becomes almost frantic at the thought of having sacrificed her son; and a young lady to whom he had just been married or betrothed, becomes quite so:—the King, overhearing the outcries that arise on the occasion, enquires into the mystery, and being stricken with admiration at the conduct of the youth and with pity at the situation of his family, makes out with an intention of sacrificing himself in return, and of exchanging himself, if possible, for his heroic friend: he accordingly delivers himself up to Fairfax, whom the author has still kept on the scene, though the General had thrown up his commission some time before. The surrender is made in consequence of a promise given to the unknown of sparing the life of young Windham in case the former should be the means of delivering up the King:—the King accordingly delivers up himself; and a good surprise is occasioned to the spectators by the supposed duplicity of Fairfax, who in apparent violation of his promise threatens to deal with both his prisoners in the same manner, and while Charles is venting his horror and indignation at the idea, gives orders that they shall both be suffered to pass the lines unmolested. The prince and his friend return to their overjoyed friends; shortly after which event Charles effects his escape in the midst of their tears and good wishes; and the piece concludes with a general chorus on their parts of Handel's anthem, "Let the King live for ever,"—a proceeding which must have been somewhat startling to the shores of Brighton,—not to mention, impolitic. The language of this piece is sufficiently commendable in general, and may be considered as a relief from the ordinary nonsense of the stage. The characters also are well kept up according to the turn the author has given them; so is the cast given to the air and habits of the republicans, except in something which Charles says about Cromwell's "gorgeous" state; and in a word, as Elliston put forth his best powers, at least on the first night of the representation, in the part of the fugitive prince, the drama altogether deserved as well as obtained success.

It is proper however to enter a strong,—perhaps an indignant protest, against the gross misrepresentation in which the author has indulged himself respecting the character of Charles II. Whether the author intended him as a sort of prototype either of the present fugitive King of Sweden or of the captive King of Spain, it is impossible to say; but whether he did or not, history ought not to have been violated. It is a question whether history ought ever to be violated in the smallest degree with respect to the characters of men;—Shakespeare certainly has helped to give additional odium to the character of Richard the Third, by fixing in the popular mind all the terrible reports respecting that usurper, and if he has been wrong in so doing,—if he has been wrong in making a bad man worse than he was, nobody can doubt that an author is still more wrong in turning a bad man into a good one, for whereas in the former instance crime is only punished a little too much, in the latter it is absolutely rewarded, and rewarded too by the only means which are left for the punishment of a guilt too high to reach during its existence,—posthumous reputation. England has suffered so many miseries from the selfish despotism of the House of Stuart,—a family which had not even the excuse of a want of sense,—that a dramatist, however prepossessed in favour of monarchs in general, ought to have thought better of his political as well as theatrical duties, before he undertook to represent in a praiseworthy and even noble light the very worst character in that House. In the dramatic Charles II. before us, the spectators see nothing but a young prince, still more interesting from his virtues than from his misfortunes, burning with the love of every thing that is great and affectionate, a hero in courage, a patriot in politics, a martyr in the cause of friendship; in short, the most brave, the most liberal, and the most noble of men. What could such of them as are ignorant of the real historical Charles say at being informed, that never was there a portrait more unlike; that this prince, so recommended and adorned, had no recommendation about him but that of an affable and easy manner, which belied his heart, and nothing respectable in his whole composition but that of a talent for wit which he abused; that even his courage, if it was never absolutely disproved, was very strongly doubted; that so far from having any patriotism in his politics, he openly endeavoured to establish absolute monarchy in the state; and so far from being grateful for kindness, or having the least real tenderness in his composition, he is acknowledged even by his panegyrists to have been one of the most selfish of mankind. It was indeed an acknowledged maxim of his, arising out of the profligacy of his habits, that as he believed nobody else to be sincere, it was his business to feel nothing for others, but as far as he could make tools of them, and this acknowledgement was the only circumstance perhaps in which he did not act the hypocrite. One of his first acts in attempting to regain his throne was the publication of a paper in which he reprobated his late father's conduct, expressed contrition for his own bad life, and pretended to be a convert to presbyterianism, and his whole existence was of a piece with this paper, a tissue of falsehoods, meannesses, and want of common decency and feeling; it is notorious, not only that he was the patron and the political parent of the execrable Jefferies, that he violated his own promises of pardon, upon which subject he expresses so much indignation against his enemy in the play,—but that, in order to maintain his unfeeling and abandoned profusion, he became the pensioner of the French king; so that of all the princes of England, he is the very last perhaps that has any claim upon the indulgence of her posterity, having been as slavish to her enemies as he was tyrannical to herself. In a word, that no false impressions may be made on the minds of those who may see this play in future, and no excuse be left for it's author, let the reader refer to any one history of Charles II. partial or impartial, and see what his own conclusions must be. Even Hume, the studious advocate of the Stuarts, and who, considered as a philosopher and a man of virtue, as he really was, treated the despotism and the profligacy of kings with a levity altogether unaccountable, is forced to confess that our romantic hero was a man who never scrupled to sacrifice his friends "to present ease or convenience" and in fine, I believe there is no reflecting and well-meaning person, of whatever side in politics, who does not think that Charles II. deserved a scaffold much more than Charles I.; for if the latter was a public tyrant by education, he was a worthy man in private, while the latter was not only a tyrant in spite of all that he had suffered and all the benefits he had received, but was an unmixed profligate in all the relations of life.
